issues.legal_issue: The authority determining a surplus area may ignore an order made by another statutory authority if that order diminishes the surplus area.
material_facts: Purchase orders were made under the tenant-purchase provision and would have removed land from the landowner’s surplus area.
The State was not a party to the purchase proceedings and had no notice or opportunity there to contest whether the purchases would diminish the surplus area.
The surplus-area authority treated the purchase orders as ineffective when determining the landowner’s surplus area.
issues.conclusion: The purchase orders could be ignored to the extent that they diminished the surplus area; “other authority” includes authorities exercising jurisdiction under the tenant-purchase provision.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10A(c) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, an order of a court or other authority obtained after the Act commenced must be ignored when it diminishes the area that could be declared surplus. “Other authority” is not confined to bodies outside the Act. Reading sections 10A and 18 harmoniously, only orders that diminish the surplus pool are affected; purchases that do not diminish it, including qualifying purchases from a tenant’s permissible area or by a tenant resettled on surplus land, are not thereby nullified. The Court overruled Mam Raj v. State of Punjab on this point.

predicates.surplus_area_determination_proceeding: An authority is determining the surplus area available for the statutory resettlement of displaced tenants.
predicates.statutory_order_reduces_surplus_area: A court or statutory authority has made an order that reduces the land available for that resettlement.

issues.definition: When an authority is determining surplus land and an order reduces that land, the surplus-area authority may disregard the order to the extent of the reduction.

issues.legal_issue: A consent order made without judicial satisfaction of statutory eligibility requirements cannot be used to defeat a statutory public purpose or bind the State enforcing it.
material_facts: The alleged tenants and the landowner were closely connected and obtained purchase orders on the basis of a compromise before an inquiry began.
The purchase orders did not show that the deciding officer had considered or found the facts required for eligibility, including the required continuous occupation.
The surplus-area authority found that the leases were collusive and that the applicants had not completed the qualifying period of occupation.
The State was not a party to the purchase proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The purchase orders were a nullity and were ineffective against the State; the State could rely on the statutory scheme to resist their use to remove the land from the surplus pool.
issues.legal_principle: Where socioeconomic legislation expresses public policy and makes relief conditional on statutory facts, parties cannot evade those conditions through a compromise order. The order may be treated as a nullity where the record does not show that the tribunal applied its mind to, and was satisfied of, the required conditions. The Court relied on K. K. Chari v. R. M. Seshadri, Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat, Kaushalya Devi v. K. L. Bansal, and Ferozi Lal Jain v. Man Mal. It also applied sections 10A and 18 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, noting that the State was not a party to the purchase proceedings and that the public resettlement interest was not represented there.

rule.if: statutory_benefit_proceeding and consent_order_grants_benefit and not_recorded_judicial_satisfaction_of_eligibility and state_not_party_to_proceeding

predicates.statutory_benefit_proceeding: A tribunal is deciding an application for a benefit that legislation makes conditional on specified facts.
predicates.consent_order_grants_benefit: The tribunal grants the requested benefit on the parties’ compromise or consent.
predicates.recorded_judicial_satisfaction_of_eligib: The record shows that the tribunal considered the evidence and was satisfied that the statutory eligibility conditions were met.
predicates.state_not_party_to_proceeding: The State, whose statutory public interest is affected, was not a party to the proceeding.

issues.definition: A consent order granting a statutory benefit is ineffective against the State when the required eligibility was not judicially established and the State did not participate.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory protection of surplus land covers leases and transfers brought about by operation of law when they diminish land available for resettlement.
material_facts: The land in dispute lay outside the landowner’s reserved area and was treated as part of the surplus area.
After the Act commenced, the landowner’s interest in the land was transferred through a gift and subsequent dealings, and new leases were claimed in favour of the applicants.
The claimed leases and purchase orders would have reduced the land available to the State for resettlement.
issues.conclusion: The statutory prohibition covers leases and can also reach transfers brought about by operation of law when they diminish the surplus area; the claimed leases could not defeat the State’s right to use the land for resettlement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10A(b) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, prevents a transfer or other disposition of land comprised in the surplus area from affecting its utilization for resettlement. A lease is a transfer or disposition of land, as reflected in section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. Read with section 10A(c), the provision protects the surplus pool against dispositions, voluntary or otherwise, that diminish it. The statutory exceptions for acquisition by the State and inheritance support the conclusion that transfers by operation of law are not categorically outside the provision.

predicates.surplus_area_protection_proceeding: An authority is applying a statutory scheme that reserves surplus land for resettling displaced tenants.
predicates.land_is_in_surplus_pool: The land forms part of the surplus land available for that statutory purpose.
predicates.disposition_or_legal_transfer_reduces_re: A lease or other disposition, including a transfer brought about by operation of law, reduces the land available for resettlement.

issues.definition: A disposition cannot defeat statutory utilization when it reduces land already in the surplus pool reserved for resettlement.

issues.legal_issue: Land held by earlier tenants does not automatically fall outside a landowner’s surplus area when those tenants give up possession, and a new tenant must meet the statutory conditions to purchase it.
material_facts: At the commencement of the Act, one disputed parcel was in the landowner’s own cultivation and two parcels were occupied by tenants.
The earlier tenants later gave up possession, and the land came into the landowner’s actual possession; the new applicants were not transferees from those earlier tenants.
There was no evidence establishing that the disputed parcels formed part of the earlier tenants’ permissible area.
The new applicants’ occupation began after the Act commenced and, on the surplus-area authority’s findings, had not lasted for the required continuous period when they applied to purchase.
The landowner had made a gift of the parcels before the claimed leases to the applicants.
issues.conclusion: The parcels were properly included in the landowner’s surplus area; the claimed new leases diminished that area and the applicants did not qualify to purchase the land under section 18.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(3) and 2(5-a) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, a tenant’s permissible area is excluded from the surplus area, but land is not excluded merely because it was once held by a tenant: it must be shown to have been within that tenant’s permissible area. Where the earlier tenancy ends and possession reverts to the landowner, a new tenant cannot claim the earlier tenant’s status merely by occupying the land later. Section 18(1) gives a purchase right to an eligible tenant, including a tenant with the required continuous occupation; Sahib Ram v. Financial Commissioner, Punjab was cited concerning the categories and qualification of tenants entitled to purchase. Sections 10A(a) and 10A(b) protect the State’s ability to use surplus land for resettlement.

rule.if: surplus_area_determination_proceeding and earlier_tenants_relinquished_possession and not_proven_within_earlier_tenants_permissible_area and new_tenant_inducted_after_reversion and not_qualified_continuous_occupation

predicates.surplus_area_determination_proceeding: An authority is determining whether land belongs in the statutory surplus pool.
predicates.earlier_tenants_relinquished_possession: The tenants occupying the land at the relevant starting point later gave up possession and the land returned to the landowner.
predicates.proven_within_earlier_tenants_permissibl: Evidence establishes that the land fell within the earlier tenants’ permissible holdings.
predicates.new_tenant_inducted_after_reversion: A different tenant began occupying the land after the earlier tenancy ended and possession returned to the landowner.
predicates.qualified_continuous_occupation: The applicant had the continuous occupation required by law when applying to purchase the tenancy.

issues.definition: When earlier tenants give up possession, the land’s exclusion from the surplus pool depends on proof that it was within their permissible holdings, and a later tenant who lacks the required continuous occupation cannot purchase it.
